source.title: Mechanistic Design and Scaling of Hybrid Architectures
source.authors: Michael Poli; Armin W. Thomas; Eric Nguyen; Pragaash Ponnusamy; Bjorn Deiseroth; K. Kersting; Taiji Suzuki; Brian L. Hie; Stefano Ermon; Christopher Ré; Ce Zhang; Stefano Massaroli

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies an IsoFLOP compute-optimal scaling analysis, estimating loss optima over parameter/token allocations as in the referenced scaling-law work, but on additional architectures and with a different experimental scope.
record.gate_note: The paper measures compute-optimal perplexity and parameter/token allocations, and compares architecture topology and batch-size settings. It does not directly fit or test the general held-out-loss power-law form or small-run power-law extrapolation. The MAD-to-perplexity correlations are reported as findings about synthetic-task prediction, not downstream-task performance.
record.test_reason: The study applies the Hoffmann-style IsoFLOP protocol (quadratic or polynomial fits per compute budget) to Transformer++ and to new convolutional, recurrent and hybrid architectures on The Pile. It reports compute-optimal model-size and token allocations versus FLOPS, a topology ablation at fixed size, and a batch-size effect on the estimated optimum. These bear on V3, V4 and V7 in a new architectural setting. It does not fit the loss power law itself (V1), test extrapolation (V2) or test downstream tasks (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that MAD synthetic-task scores correlate with compute-optimal perplexity, enabling cheap architecture prototyping. They find hybrid (striped, MoE, Hyena-expert) architectures beat Transformer++, Hyena and Mamba in compute-optimal and overtrained scaling, with up to 20% lower perplexity at equal compute. Further conclusions: about 25% attention is the optimal hybrid ratio; perplexity follows a power law in state size; optimal token/parameter allocation is fairly stable but skews toward data for efficient models; architecture rankings change between text and byte-level DNA.
record.recipe_differences: The paper expands the compute-optimal IsoFLOP approach to emerging and hybrid architectures, uses The Pile, and estimates optima with polynomial fits to observed training perplexities. It does not directly fit the general loss power-law form or test small-run extrapolation.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture affects estimated parameter/token allocation; topology changes perplexity; batch-size scaling shifts the compute-efficient frontier and estimated optimum; architecture rankings differ between subword language data and byte-level DNA data.

fits_no_version.finding: Aggregate MAD synthetic-task accuracy correlates linearly with compute-optimal Pile perplexity within the Hyena family and for Mamba vs Striped Mamba. Correlation is noisier across architecture classes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small-model synthetic token-manipulation scores rank architectures' compute-optimal pretraining perplexity.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute-optimal perplexity scales with total state size as P* proportional to M^c, c about -0.28, consistent across architectures; model class sets the offset (Finding 8, Fig 4.3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal perplexity follows a power law in recurrent/cache state dimension with an architecture-independent exponent.

fits_no_version.finding: Architecture rankings flip between subword text and byte-level DNA: Transformer++ is worst on DNA at all IsoFLOP groups and degrades most when overtrained.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The relative scaling of architecture classes depends on data domain and tokenization.

fits_no_version.finding: The off-optimal perplexity gap is proportional to the hybridization ratio. Hybrids have flatter IsoFLOP curves than Transformers (Finding 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sensitivity of loss to off-compute-optimal allocation depends on architecture.

record.problems: The paper does not report numerical allocation exponents in the cited text, and several relevant trends are available only in figures. The topology ablation reports no uncertainty estimates. The MAD-to-perplexity correlations have no numerical correlation coefficients stated here; the authors note that cross-architecture correlations are noisier.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out; all 12 topology-ablation values in Table D.1 are included.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in N, D or C is reported. Compute-optimal perplexity vs FLOPS is plotted (Fig 1.1C, 4.3) but no functional form is fitted or stated.
No extrapolation from small-run fits to much larger runs.
No numeric exponents, no direct comparison to the Kaplan vs Hoffmann split. Allocation fits in Fig 4.1 span only 4e18 to 8e19 FLOPs.
Depth/width aspect ratio at fixed parameter count is not varied; only hybrid layer ordering at one size and budget.
The power-law form is not established for byte-level DNA (no fit reported). No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer settings.
No comparison of fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions or published laws. No evidence of curvature away from a power law.

missing.what: Compute-optimal perplexity vs FLOPS frontier per architecture (plotted log-log, up to about 2e21 FLOPs; no fit stated). It is the closest the paper comes to V1.
Compute-optimal model size and token count vs FLOPS for four architectures on byte-level DNA (figure only).
Attention-ratio sweep at fixed compute: 25% attention optimal; 0% and 100% clearly worse across all IsoFLOP groups. Shows primitive mix, unlike ordering, changes loss substantially.
State-optimal exponent c about -0.28 across architectures.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche is T3 rather than T1: the IsoFLOP method matches Hoffmann, but the results are mainly on new architectures and topologies. Allocation results are figure-only, with no exponents. The extracted fit range for Fig 4.1 (4e18 to 8e19) is only about 1.3 orders of magnitude, though Appendix C lists groups up to 2e21. On V4, the reader labelled the topology ablation 'limits_scope' based on the authors' word 'significant'. I relabel it 'supports', since the measured spread is about 3% at fixed size. This V4 support should not be extended to changes of primitive type, which move perplexity far more (Fig 4.2, 20% gains). DNA rows (r23, r24) are unlinked from V5 because no power-law fit on DNA is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study evaluates perplexity across model sizes and compute budgets, but does not test whether held-out loss follows a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute when other factors are not bottlenecks.
It does not fit power laws on small training runs and use those fits to predict much larger runs.

The study examines compute-optimal parameter and token allocations across its tested architectures and compute budgets, but does not establish the claimed general growth rates across other setups or datasets.
It tests topology choices for a 750M StripedHyena model, not a broad range of depth, width, or architecture changes at fixed parameter count.
It reports byte-level/DNA scaling and overtraining results, but does not test image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The paper does not evaluate downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.

It shows that batch-size scaling affects the estimated compute-efficient frontier, but does not systematically compare exponent-fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, or the published laws, nor does it establish general curve bending away from power laws.

statements.correction: Dataset: The Pile; sequence length: 8k; Figure 4.1 budgets: 4e18–8e19 FLOPS; allocation estimates: figure only, without numerical exponents or a stated token/parameter ratio; Finding 5: aT > aH and bT < bH.
statements.problem: This study uses The Pile, not DCLM, and does not state an approximately 20-token/parameter Transformer allocation or a constant token/parameter ratio. Its numerical allocation exponents are not reported.
